body.p: After entry of this Response, claims 1-7, 9-20, and 22-26 are pending in the patent application. Claims 8 and 21 have been cancelled without prejudice or disclaimer, claims 1- 2, 5, 9-13, 16, 19, 22-23, and 25 are currently amended, and no claims have been newly added. Applicant's attorney respectfully requests reconsideration of, and favorable action regarding, claims 1-7, 9-20, and 22-26 in view of this Response, which adds no new matter to the patent application.
Claim Interpretation of "Illumination Unit" and "Acquisition Unit" Under 35 U.S.C. 4 112(f)
Not only is the examiner's interpretation of "an illumination unit" as a "generic

placeholder that is coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to perform the recited function and the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier" incorrect, but Applicant does not understand how the examiner can so interpret "an illumination unit" in view of the structural description of "an illumination unit" in the patent application. FIG. 1 and paragraph [0028] of the patent application, which paragraph the examiner cited and quoted only partially, recites:
[0028] Starting from the imaging probe 127, it has an illumination unit (for
illuminating the field of view 103) and an acquisition unit for acquiring
images in the field of view (103) that comprise the following components. In
the illumination unit, an excitation light source 133 and a white light source
136 generate an excitation light and a white light, respectively. The excitation
light has wavelength and energy suitable to excite the fluorophores of the fluorescence agent (such as of Near Infra-Red, or NIR, type), whereas the
white light appears substantially colorless to the human eye (such as

containing all the wavelengths of the spectrum that is visible to the human eye at equal intensity). Corresponding delivery optics 139 and delivery optics 142 deliver the excitation light and the white light, respectively, to the (same) field
of view 103.
"Illumination unit" by itself recites sufficient structure to avoid a "means plus

function" interpretation because the recitation of "for applying an excitation light adapted to exciting the luminescence substance" inherently describes a light (structure) for generating a specified type of light (a light that can excite the luminescence substance).
But even assuming, arguendo, that "illumination unit," by itself, does not recite

sufficient structure to avoid a "means plus function" interpretation, paragraph [0028] of the patent application discloses structural "components" (e.g., excitation light source 133, white light source 136, delivery optics 139 and delivery optics 142) of the "illumination unit" sufficient to avoid a means-plus-function interpretation of "illumination unit" under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f).
A similar analysis and reasoning applies to the claim-24 term "acquisition unit,"
which is in FIG. 1 of the patent application, and about which paragraph [0028] of the patent application states:
In the acquisition unit, collection optics 145 collect light from the field of view
103 (in an epi-illumination geometry).

In view of the preceding analysis and reasoning, Applicant requests the examiner to interpret the claim-24 terms "illumination unit" and "acquisition unit" under standard claim- interpretation guidelines, not under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f).
Without acquiescing to the propriety of this rejection, Applicant has amended claim 23 in a manner that overcomes this rejection as set forth below.
The examiner rejected claim 23 as allegedly failing to recite a combination of elements supporting the claimed function.

Claim 23 has been amended to remove "means," and to specify the elements used to perform the corresponding steps of claim 1 (see claim 1 as amended, "A method for imaging a region of interest of a patient for a medical procedure performed thereon, wherein the method comprises, under the control of a computing device," see the patent application, p. 11, lines 16-22, "With reference now to FIG.3, the main software components are shown that may be used to implement the solution according to an embodiment of the present disclosure. ... The software components 300 are typically stored in the mass memory and loaded (at least in part) into the working memory of the central unit of the imaging system when the programs are running," and see the patent application p. 44, lines 16-17, "However, the computing device may be of any type (for example, a central unit of an imaging system, a separate computer and so on).").

Particularly, claim 23 has been amended to recite "a luminescence drive for ..." (see the patent application, p. 11, line 29 through page 12, line 2, "A fluorescence drive 305 drives a fluorescence unit of the imaging system (comprising the excitation light source and the fluorescence camera) dedicated to acquiring the fluorescence images of the field of view suitable illuminated for this purpose," and see the patent application, p. 33, lines 1-5, "However, the luminescence substance may be of any extrinsic/intrinsic or exogenous/endogenous type (for example, any luminescence agent, any natural luminescence component, based on any luminescence phenomenon, such as fluorescence, phosphorescence, chemiluminescence, bio-luminescence, induced Raman-radiation, and so on).").
Claim 23 has been amended further to recite "an auxiliary drive for ..." (see the

patent application, p. 12, lines 12-15, "Likewise, a reflectance drive 315 drives a reflectance unit of the imaging system (comprising the white light source and the reflectance camera) dedicated to acquiring the reflectance images of the field of view suitable illuminated for this purpose," and p. 34, lines 1-3, "the auxiliary light may be of any type different from the luminescence light of the luminescence image (for example, visible light, IR light, Ultra- Violet (UV) light, other luminescence light at different wavelength and so on).").
Claim 23 has been amended also to recite "a segmenter for ..." (see the patent
application, p. 13, lines 2-4, "A segmenter 335 segments the prepared reflectance images (semantically) into their informative regions and non-informative regions;").

Claim 23 has been amended to recite "an adapter for ..." (see the patent application, p. 13, line 31 through page 14, line 2, "An adapter 355 optionally adapts the reflectance segmentation masks and the reflectance equalization maps to the fluorescence images, so as to equalize their sizes and to synchronize them.").

Claim 23 has been amended to recite "a processor for ..." (see the patent application, p. 14, lines 17-19, "A processor 370 (post-)processes the fluorescence images limited to their informative regions for facilitating the identification of the representation of the tumor therein (for example, by auto-scaling and/or thresholding them).").

Claim 23 has been amended further to recite "an output drive for ..." (see the patent application, p. 15, lines 6-8, "A monitor drive 390 drives the monitor of the imaging system to display the output images (substantially in real-time during the surgical procedure)," and see the patent application, p. 35, lines 14-18, "However, the output image may be of any type (for example, the same processed luminescence image, the processed luminescence image
combined/overlaid with the reflectance image, and so on) and it may be output in any way (for example, displayed, printed, transmitted remotely, in real-time or off-line, and so on).").

Claim 1 has been amended to recite "wherein the processed luminescence image provides for facilitating an identification of a further representation of the target body thereinfacilitating an identification thereof," so as to clarify that the processed luminescence image provides a further representation of the target body different from the one in the luminescence image, for example, resulting from its auto-scaling (see the patent application, p. 9, line 26 through p. 10, line 20) or thresholding (see p. 10, line 21 through p. 11, line 8) and then the target body is identified in this further representation thereof.
The examiner rejected claim 2 as being indefinite with respect to the "surgical procedure."

Claim 2 has been amended to recite "wherein the method is for assisting the medical procedure is a surgical procedure on the patient," (see the patent application, p. 32, lines 2-4, "However, the method may be used for assisting any medical procedure (for example, a surgical procedure, a diagnostic procedure, a therapeutic procedure and so on).").
The examiner rejected claim 5 as allegedly being indefinite with respect to the "medical tools."

Claim 5 has been amended to recite "wherein the foreign objects comprise one or more medical instrumentsimplements, one or more hands, one or more medical tools," so as to use a common word for both instruments and tools (see Gemini, "What is an implement? An implement is a tool or instrument used to carry out a task or achieve a specific purpose.").
The examiner rejected claim 21 as being indefinite with respect to the "computing device."
This rejection has been rendered moot by the cancellation of claim 21.
The examiner rejected claim 22 as allegedly being indefinite with respect to the "computing device."

Claim 22 has been amended to clarify the presence of a single computing device (see the patent application, p. 11, lines 16-22, "With reference now to FIG.3, the main software components are shown that may be used to implement the solution according to an embodiment of the present disclosure... The software components 300 are typically stored in the mass memory and loaded (at least in part) into the working memory of the central unit of the imaging system when the programs are running," and p. 44, lines 16-17, "However, the computing device may be of any type (for example, a central unit of an imaging system, a separate computer and so on).").
The examiner objected to claim 23 as allegedly being indefinite with respect to the "computing device."
Claim 23 has been amended to clarify the presence of a single computing device (see above).
The examiner objected to claim 25 as being indefinite with respect to features recited in claim 1.
Claim 25 has been amended to clarify the presence of a single instance of each feature.

Rejection of Claims 1-26 Under 35 U.S.C. 4 101 Without acquiescing to the propriety of this rejection, Applicant has amended some of claims 1-26 in a manner that overcomes this rejection for all of claims 1-26.
The examiner rejected claim 21 as allegedly being directed to a non-statutory subject matter.
This rejection has been rendered moot by the cancellation of claim 21.
The examiner rejected claim 22 as allegedly being directed to a non-statutory subject matter as encompassing a transitory form of signal transmission.

Claim 22 has been amended to recite "A computer program product comprising one or more non-transitory computer readable storage media" (see the patent application, p. 43, lines 24-26, "The storage medium is any tangible medium (different from transitory signals per se) that may retain and store instructions for use by the computing device.").
The examiner rejected claim 1 as allegedly being directed to an abstract idea due to at least some recitations of claim 1 allegedly being capable of being performed in the human mind.

Claim 1 has been amended to recite "A method for assistingimaging a region of interest of a patient for a medical procedure performed thereon, wherein the method comprises, under the control of a computing device: acquiring, by the computing device, a luminescence image of a field of view containing the region of interest for the medical procedure of the patient," (see the patent application, p. 15, lines 15-16, "Starting from FIG.4A-FIG.4B, their activity diagram represents an exemplary process that may be used to imaging a patient with a method 400.").
This amendment clarifies that claim 1, as a whole, integrates all the recited features in a practical application (i.e., medical imaging) that is not directed to a judicial exception.
In addition, claim 1 has been amended to recite "identifyingsegmenting, by the

computing device, the auxiliary values of the auxiliary image semantically into at least one region of interest class defining an auxiliary informative region of the auxiliary image representative of the region of interest without the foreign objects according to a content of the auxiliary image and one or more foreign object classes defining a non-informative region representative of the foreign objects," (see the patent application, p. 18, lines 7-11, "In this specific case, the semantic segmentation is aimed at partitioning the reflectance image into the informative region representing the surgical cavity without the foreign objects and the non-informative region representing the foreign objects (i.e., surgical instruments, hands, surgical tools, surrounding body-parts and/or background materials)").

Claim 1 has been amended further to recite "identifying, by the computing device, the luminescence values of the luminescence image defining a luminescence informative region of the luminescence image corresponding to the auxiliary values of the auxiliary informative region of the auxiliary image," (see the patent application, p. 21, lines 8-12, "In any case, the adapter adds the fluorescence segmentation mask and the fluorescence equalization map (equal to the reflectance segmentation mask and to the reflectance equalization map, respectively, possibly adapted to the fluorescence image) to the corresponding repositories.").
Claim 1 also has been amended to recite "the processing of theprocessed

luminescence image comprising a plurality of processed luminescence values being based on the luminescence values of the luminescence informative regions" (see the patent application, p. 22, line 25 through page 23, line 10, "If the label is asserted (meaning that the pixel belongs to the informative region), the processor at block 442 converts the corresponding

pixel value by applying the informative mapping function and adds it to the same cell of a (new) auto-scaled fluorescence image (in a corresponding temporary variable)" and p. 23, lines 13-31, "If the label is asserted (meaning that the pixel belongs to the informative region), the processor at block 454 compares the corresponding pixel value with the threshold value. If the pixel value is (possibly strictly) higher than the threshold value (i.e., it belongs to the target segment), the processor at block 456 copies it to the same cell of a (new) thresholded fluorescence image (in a corresponding temporary variable). Conversely, if the pixel value is (possibly strictly) lower than the threshold value (i.e., it belongs to the non-target segment), the processor at block 458 resets the pixel value in the same cell of the thresholded fluorescence image to zero (so as to mask it).").
Claims 22-23 and 25 have been amended in a similar manner.
The remaining claims are directed to statutory subject matter by virtue of their dependencies from an independent claim directed to statutory subject matter.

Regarding claim 1, Kishima et al. proposes acquiring and storing a fluorescence

image of an entire surgical field SA in which an operator is not interested, for example, for confirming complete removal of a cancer (see Kishima's paragraph 0009, "there is a need to confirm, during or after the surgery, whether or not cancer cells that have not been removed exist") or for a possible medical malpractice suit (see Kishima's paragraph 0059 "Therefore, it is possible to prepare for a market of countermeasures against a medical malpractice suit, for example"); however, an ROI area of the fluorescence image in which the operator is actually interested is enlarged (by digital zooming) and the ROI area is then displayed (see Kishima's paragraph 0059, "The fluorescence navigation surgery system according to this embodiment is capable of enlarging an image of the area ROI in which the operator is interested by digital zooming in response to a user's request and displaying the image, and capturing and storing an image of the entire surgical filed SA with a pixel resolution in which a tumor is not missed. Therefore, it is possible to capture an image of an area in which the operator is not interested, which is not captured in the typical system, and to store the image."). The fluorescence image shows only a fluorescence area FA wherein a fluorescent contrast medium collects (see Kashima's paragraph 0048, "As shown in FIG. 2, on the monitor for fluorescence image observation 16, the area ROI including the fluorescence area FA, in which the operator is interested, is enlarged and displayed, for example"). At the same time, a visible light image of the surgical field SA is acquired (see Kashima's paragraph 0032, "The video camera for surgical field observation 1 is capable of capturing an image of the entire surgicalfield SA"), wherein the fluorescence area FA is instead not visible (see Kashima's paragraph 0033, "the fluorescence area FA is not displayed on the monitor for surgicalfield observation 3").
In a first embodiment of Kishima, the fluorescence image (of the ROI area) is

displayed on a monitor 16 (see Kishima's paragraph 0047, "display a fluorescence image of only the area ROI ... on the monitor for fluorescence image observation 16") and the visible light image (of the surgical field SA) is displayed on another monitor 3 (see Kishima's paragraph 0033, "the entire surgical field SA is displayed on the monitor for surgical field

observation 3"). In a second embodiment, the visible light image of the ROI area is captured by digital zooming (see Kishima's paragraph 0076, "performing optical zooming with the optical zoom lens 2 to capture an image of only the area ROI in which the operator is interested"); the fluorescence image and the visible light image (both of them of the ROI area) are then superimposed and displayed on a single monitor 16B (see Kishima's paragraph 0073, "two images are superimposed and the superimposed image is observed on a monitor in the second embodiment. It should be noted that the second embodiment is the same as the first embodiment in that the area ROI in which the operator is interested is displayed"). A

third embodiment simply differs in that the fluorescence image and the visual light image are captured from the same optical axis (see Kishima's paragraph 0085, "the image is captured from the same optical axis direction").

In contrast, claim 1 is directed to the computing device automatically segmenting the auxiliary image into the auxiliary informative region (representative of the region of interest without the foreign objects) and the non-informative region (representative of the foreign objects).

Conversely, in Kishima et al. the ROI area is selected manually by the operator (see Kishima's paragraph 0021, "cause a user to select at least a partial area of the observation target area and to capture a visible light image of the selected area as a ROI area"). In any case, to the contrary of the subject matter recited in claim 1, in Kishima et al. the ROI area is expressly selected to comprise the foreign objects as well (see Kishima's paragraph 0032, "the video camera for surgical field observation 1 needs to capture an image of the operator's handling of a needle accurately").

Moreover, claim 1 is directed to the computing device generating the processed luminescence image by processing the luminescence image limited to the luminescence informative region, so as to provide a different representation of the target body, thus facilitating its identification.

Conversely, in Kishima et al., the fluorescence image and the visual light image are simply aligned and then superimposed (see Kishima's paragraph 0021, "generate a superimposed image by aligning a position of the visible light image with a position of the cut fluorescence image and superimposing the images"). Therefore, the representation of the fluorescence area FA remains the same as in the fluorescence image.

Starting from Kishima et al. and even taking into account Snyder at al. (being cited by the examiner against claim 8, the subject matter of which is now substantially incorporated into claim 1) it is not possible to attain the proposed solution.
In fact, Snyder et al. simply mentions the use of segmentation for identifying corresponding elements in images.

However, Snyder et al. is completely silent about any identification of a luminescence informative region of a luminescence image corresponding to an auxiliary informative region of an auxiliary image (resulting from its segmentation), let alone the generation of any processed luminescence image by processing the luminescence image limited to the luminescence informative region so as to provide a different representation of the target body facilitating its identification.

In any case, Snyder et al. teaches away from the subject matter recited in claim 1. In fact, in relation to claim 1, the auxiliary informative region (determined on the auxiliary image to represent the region of interest without the foreign objects) is transferred to the luminescence image so as to process it by taking into account only the representation of the region of interest for the medical procedure (i.e., the surgical cavity), instead disregarding the representation of the foreign objects around and/or overlapping it (comprising the surgical instruments/tools).
Conversely, Snyder et al. is aimed at tracking instruments/tools (see Snyder's

paragraph 0055, "According to various embodiments, the navigation system 26 can be used to track the instrument 68 relative to the patient 30") used during a surgical procedure (see Snyder's paragraph 0038, "The tool 68 may be any appropriate tool such as a drill, forceps, or other tool operated by the user 72"). Therefore, contrary to the subject matter recited in claim 1 and in other claims, in Snyder et al. it is the instruments/tools that are displayed (see Snyder's paragraph 0042, "When navigating the instrument 68, a position of the instrument 68 can be illustrated relative to image data acquired of the patient 30 on a display device 84").

Claims 22-23 and 25 are patentable for reasons similar to those set forth above in conjunction with claim 1, and the dependent claims are patentable at least by virtue of the dependencies from an independent claim.

In view of the foregoing amendments and remarks, Applicant requests reconsideration of the patent application and a Notice of Allowance for the pending claims. If any issues remain that prevent issuance of this application, Examiner is urged to contact me before issuing a subsequent Action. Please call or email me at your convenience.
